title: Coomer v. Lindell — Rule 11 Sanctions for AI-Generated Defective Citations ($3,000 Each, July 2025) and Repeat Sanction ($5,000, May 2026)
author: Judge Nina Y. Wang

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: Coomer accepts the cluster’s core proposition that established human filing duties govern AI-assisted litigation and materially extends it with another Rule 11 example involving misrepresented authority, nonexistent cases, delegated citation checking, and a show-cause process. It also reinforces that AI is not the exclusive source of citation defects and does not establish final sanctions from the supplied excerpts.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between fabricated citations and misleading uses of genuine authorities. It applies existing Rule 11 duties to misrepresented holdings or legal significance and treats careless AI use as a well-known risk without claiming that AI uniquely causes citation errors or establishing an empirical error rate.
qs: “Misrepresenting the legal significance of a case” may also  violate Rule 11.

Although these errors can occur without the use of AI,  the   nationwide    “rash   of   cases”   involving   AI-generated    hallucinations    and  misrepresentations have made the risks of careless AI use well known.

st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: Coomer directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI-assisted filings remain governed by Rule 11’s existing reasonable-inquiry and human-verification duties. It also aligns with the cluster’s treatment of responsibility as participation-specific and sanctions as procedurally constrained and proportionate.
qs: In other words, Rule 11 imposes an “affirmative duty” on an  attorney to conduct a reasonable inquiry into the legal basis for a filing before submitting  it.

And because Rule 11(b) demands a reasonable  inquiry, “[a] litigant’s using AI and then failing to verify the accuracy of the results it yields  violates the litigant’s [Rule] 11 obligations.” Willis, 2025 WL 1224273, at *3.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that existing human filing and reasonable-inquiry duties persist when lawyers use AI. Its sanctions analysis focuses on counsel’s failure to verify defective authorities and extends responsibility to individual lawyers and the firm, rather than treating AI use itself as sanctionable.

kp.k: AI-assisted briefing produced extensive defects beyond fabricated cases
kp.d: The April 23, 2025 show-cause order identified nearly thirty defective citations in defendants’ February 25 opposition to a motion in limine. The defects included fabricated cases, misquotations, unsupported descriptions of legal principles, and misidentification of courts and binding authority. Kachouroff admitted using generative AI and not personally checking the resulting citations. These are findings about particular filings, not measured model error rates.
qs: the Court identified nearly thirty defective citations in the Opposition.
MR. KACHOUROFF: Your Honor, I personally did not check it. I am responsible for it not being checked.

These defects include but are not limited to misquotes of cited cases; misrepresentations of principles of law associated with cited cases, including discussions of legal principles that simply do not appear within such decisions; misstatements regarding whether case law originated from a binding authority such as the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit; misattributions of case law to this District; and most egregiously, citation of cases that do not exist.

kp.k: Existing Rule 11 duties govern AI-assisted legal work
kp.d: The July 2025 order applied Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b)(2), rather than a new AI-specific rule: counsel must reasonably investigate whether legal contentions are supported by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument for legal change. The May 2026 order reiterated that failing to verify AI results violates this duty, quoting Willis. AI assistance does not remove counsel’s responsibility for submissions.
qs: recognize that Rule 11 applies to the use of artificial intelligence.
Rule 11 imposes an “affirmative duty” on an attorney to conduct a reasonable inquiry into the legal basis for a filing before submitting it.
“[a] litigant’s using AI and then failing to verify the accuracy of the results it yields violates the litigant’s [Rule] 11 obligations.”

kp.k: Delegating citation checks does not transfer professional responsibility
kp.d: Kachouroff said he delegated citation checking to co-counsel Jennifer DeMaster; both signed the defective opposition. The court held that blind reliance on another attorney can improperly delegate a nondelegable Rule 11 responsibility. The July order also applied Rule 11’s presumptive joint responsibility for a lawyer’s firm.
qs: blind reliance on another attorney can be an improper delegation of an attorney’s nondelegable responsibility under Rule 11.
“Absent exceptional circumstances, a law firm must be held jointly responsible for a violation committed by its partner, associate, or employee.”

kp.k: Documentary evidence undermined counsel’s wrong-draft explanation
kp.d: Counsel attributed the defective filing to accidentally submitting an earlier draft rather than a thoroughly checked final version. The July order rejected that explanation based on emails, exchanged drafts, document naming, and persistent substantive errors. The Westlaw report concerned the substantially defective version, not the purportedly correct version; the record did not establish that the corrected document was ready at filing. This finding distinguished claimed verification from documented review.
qs: Put simply, neither defense counsel’s communications nor the “final” version of the Opposition that they reviewed corroborate the existence of the “correct” version.
The “correct” version of the Opposition still has substantive errors
Ms. DeMaster ran the Westlaw report on a different version.

kp.k: Verification must address legal substance, not merely case existence
kp.d: The orders treated misrepresented holdings and court attribution as substantive defects even when a cited case existed. In the May 2026 order, Capital Solutions was incorrectly presented as Tenth Circuit authority supporting finality of punitive damages under the Reexamination Clause. The court explained that it was a district court decision about initial jury determination under the trial-by-jury clause, while Supreme Court precedent contradicted the asserted Reexamination Clause proposition.
qs: In and of itself, falsely citing a district court case as binding authority is a “material” error.
The Response misstates both Capital Solutions’s holding and the applicable Seventh Amendment law.
Capital Solutions addressed Cooper Industries and expressly disclaimed any reliance on the Reexamination Clause.

kp.k: July sanctions allocated liability to counsel, not clients
kp.d: On July 7, 2025, the court imposed $3,000 on Kachouroff and McSweeney Cynkar & Kachouroff PLLC jointly and severally, and a separate $3,000 on DeMaster individually. It described these as the least severe sanctions adequate to deter and punish the conduct. It declined to sanction Lindell, FrankSpeech, or My Pillow because Kachouroff confirmed he had not advised defendants of his use of AI tools in his practice.
qs: a sanction of $3,000 against Christopher I. Kachouroff and the law firm of McSweeney Cynkar & Kachouroff PLLC, jointly and severally, and $3,000 against Ms. DeMaster, individually, is the least severe sanction adequate to deter and punish defense counsel in this instance.
this Court does not extend the sanctions to Defendants

kp.k: Repeat sanction did not require established AI causation
kp.d: The May 7, 2026 order expressed skepticism about Kachouroff’s explanation of the Capital Solutions errors, but grounded its Rule 11 finding in unreasonable review regardless of whether AI generated them. Kachouroff asserted that he had cite-checked and used no generative AI to create the response except Westlaw for legal research. The court credited evidence that he alone prepared the response and discharged the show-cause order as to DeMaster and Frankspeech.
qs: I did not use any Generative Artificial Intelligence program to create Document 404 with the exception of Westlaw which I used solely for the purpose of legal research.

As an officer of the court, Mr. Kachouroff submitted yet another Response containing a materially incorrect citation that should have been corrected through a reasonable review, regardless of whether it was initially AI-generated or not.
The Second Order to Show Cause [Doc. 413] is DISCHARGED as to Jennifer DeMaster and Frankspeech LLC;

kp.k: Repeated verification failures increased the deterrent sanction
kp.d: The May 2026 order imposed an additional $5,000 jointly and severally on Kachouroff and his firm, bringing his cumulative sanction in this case to $8,000. Although the new errors were less pervasive, the court considered them no less serious and emphasized prior sanctions in this case and Pelishek. It declined a Virginia Bar referral specifically in reliance on his representation that health issues had led him to step back from active trial litigation.
qs: The Court cannot conclude that excusing this conduct as less pervasive or even repeating the previous sanction of $3,000 is sufficient to deter this conduct in the future.
the Court finds that an additional, moderately increased monetary sanction of $5,000 is sufficient to deter Mr. Kachouroff and similarly situated individuals from engaging in this conduct.
The Court will not refer Mr. Kachouroff to the Virginia Bar for disciplinary proceedings.
The Court observes that Mr. Kachouroff’s cumulative sanction in this case of $8,000 remains well within the normal range for attorneys engaging in similar conduct.

kp.k: AI citation failures implicate competence, diligence, and public trust
kp.d: The April order invoked Colorado’s professional-conduct duties of competence, diligence, and candor, noting corresponding Virginia and Wisconsin rules. The May 2026 order framed enforcement as protecting courts’ administration of justice and public confidence, not merely correcting technical citation mistakes. These professional-conduct concerns are distinct from the Rule 11 findings actually supporting the monetary sanctions.
qs: A lawyer shall provide competent representation to a client.
A lawyer shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.

The judiciary undermines its own central purpose of administering justice for the public good—and the public’s confidence in the institution—when it permits attorneys to breach their duties, including diligence and candor, owed to the court and the public without consequence.

kp.k: Court situated escalating sanctions within broader judicial responses
kp.d: The May 2026 order reported other courts’ sanctions and shared their concern that modest financial penalties may inadequately deter careless AI-assisted argument preparation. It quoted Benjamin’s $1,500–$15,000 range for AI-generated citation cases and cited an Oregon $15,000 sanction plus fees and expenses. These are judicially cited examples and deterrence judgments, not a systematic estimate of prevalence or proof of sanction effectiveness.
qs: “courts have imposed monetary sanctions ranging from $1,500 to $15,000.”
this Court shares other courts’ concern that relatively modest monetary sanctions are insufficient to “deter attorneys from haphazardly using AI tools to craft legal arguments,”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Nina Y. Wang treats careless AI-assisted drafting as a source of materially defective legal submissions, not as an exception to lawyers’ existing duties of verification and reasonable inquiry.
pts.d: The orders describe fabricated cases, invented quotations, unsupported descriptions of holdings, and misattribution of decisions to binding courts in an AI-assisted brief. Wang holds that lawyers remain responsible under Rule 11 for the legal contentions they submit; blind reliance on co-counsel can improperly delegate that responsibility. The May 2026 order also expresses concern that modest sanctions may not deter careless AI use and increases the monetary sanction for repeated conduct. These are case-specific findings and deterrence judgments, rather than predictions about employment, pricing, or market structure. Importantly, Wang does not conclusively establish that AI generated the second defective submission: the second sanction rests on inadequate reasonable review regardless of its origin.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of the litigation record, counsel’s admissions, examination of cited authorities and document versions, and analogous sanctions decisions—not model benchmarks or measured hallucination rates.
pts.d: For the first sanction, Wang identifies nearly thirty defective citations and cites Kachouroff’s admission that he used generative AI without personally checking the resulting citations. The court compares filed and purportedly corrected drafts, emails, document metadata, and the Westlaw report to reject counsel’s explanation that a fully corrected brief existed before filing. For the second sanction, Wang examines the Capital Solutions citation and explains both its incorrect attribution to the Tenth Circuit and its misrepresented holding. The orders also rely on similar conduct in Pelishek and sanctions in other cases. References to a nationwide rash or epidemic of AI citation incidents derive from cited judicial authorities; they are not original statistical findings by Wang.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source documents sanctions in July 2025 and May 2026, with verification required before filing and greater deterrence considered necessary after recurrence.
pts.d: The first defective brief was filed on February 25, 2025, followed by the April 23 show-cause order and July 7 sanctions order. The May 7, 2026 order addresses a later post-trial brief filed after the initial sanctions. The operative condition is a failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances, not AI use alone. The court distinguishes material misrepresentations from demands for citation perfection and acknowledges that similar errors can arise without AI. Its expectation that an additional $5,000 will deter future conduct is prospective and not evidence that deterrence subsequently occurred. The decision against disciplinary referral specifically relies on counsel’s representation that he had stepped back from active trial litigation because of health issues.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate consequences fall on litigation counsel and their firm, while the court connects inadequate verification to the administration of justice and public confidence.
pts.d: In July 2025, Wang imposes $3,000 jointly and severally on Kachouroff and McSweeney Cynkar & Kachouroff PLLC, plus $3,000 individually on DeMaster. The defendants are not sanctioned, with the court pointing to Kachouroff’s statement that he had not advised them of his AI-tool use. In May 2026, the court imposes an additional $5,000 jointly and severally on Kachouroff and the firm, bringing their cumulative sanction in this case to $8,000. DeMaster and Frankspeech are discharged from the second show-cause proceeding because the court credits their lack of involvement in preparing that submission. More broadly, Wang identifies lawyers as officers of the court whose diligence and candor support fair administration of justice and public trust.
